Types of Truck Accidents

There are several reasons for truck accidents. Regardless of their cause, all truck accidents are potentially deadly and dangerous to others, both in the crash and the immediate vicinity. The following are the most common types of truck accidents:
Jackknife accidents:
A jackknife accident happens when a tractor-trailer’s cab and trailer come together to form a “V” shape, nearly bending the truck in half.
Rear-end accidents:
Commercial trucks are prone to rear-end other vehicles as they are heavy and difficult to stop.
Underride accidents:
An underride accident occurs when a vehicle driving behind a commercial truck runs into the back of the truck and slides underneath the truck.
Rollover accidents:
A rollover accident is when a truck rolls over onto its side and often slides a considerable distance.
Blindspot accidents:
Commercial trucks have a blind spot at the rear and sides of the truck, making other vehicles challenging to see, and trucks can collide with these vehicles.
UPS Truck Accident

: When one of those drivers causes an accident, the injured victim is not dealing with an individual. They are dealing with a corporation backed by experienced adjusters and defense attorneys whose job is to limit the company’s payments.
FedEx Truck Accident

: A FedEx truck accident claim is not like a typical car accident case. FedEx is a large corporation with its own response team, which often reaches the accident scene before the injured party has even spoken to a lawyer.
Amazon Truck Accident

: Denver streets see Amazon delivery vehicles nearly every hour of the day. Vans weave through residential neighborhoods, merge onto I-25 and I-70, and navigate congested corridors like Federal Boulevard and Colfax under tight delivery windows, leaving little room for error.
Garbage Truck Accident
: Most people never think about garbage trucks until one changes their life. These vehicles move through Denver neighborhoods every morning, quiet and routine, until something goes wrong.
Tow Truck Accident

: These accidents are among the most violent collisions on Denver’s roads. Tow trucks operate in high-pressure conditions alongside fast-moving traffic on I-25 and I-70, and when a driver fails to move over, secures a load improperly, or misjudges a merge, the results can be catastrophic.
None of the above truck accidents is the same as a
car accident

. There is a vast size and weight difference involved, and multiple parties may face liability. An experienced truck accident attorney is invaluable in helping to determine all the liable parties in a truck accident as well as all possible sources of recovery for the accident victims.
Examples of Compensation in Truck Accident Cases

Truck accidents often leave victims facing far more than just vehicle damage. Serious injuries can lead to months of medical treatment, time away from work, and lasting physical and emotional challenges. While every case is different, compensation in a truck accident claim is meant to help cover the financial and personal losses caused by the crash.
Some common examples of compensation in truck accident cases include:
Medical Expenses:
Compensation may cover emergency treatment, hospital stays, surgeries, medication, physical therapy, rehabilitation, and future medical care related to your injuries.
Lost Wages and Reduced Earning Capacity:
If your injuries prevent you from working, you may be able to recover compensation for lost income, missed career opportunities, and future earnings.
Pain and Suffering:
Truck accidents can cause significant physical pain, emotional distress, anxiety, and trauma that impact daily life long after the crash.
Permanent Disabilities:
Severe injuries such as spinal cord damage or traumatic brain injuries may require lifelong care and support, which can be included in a settlement or verdict.
Property Damage:
Victims may also recover the cost of repairing or replacing their vehicle and other personal property damaged in the collision.
Loss of Enjoyment of Life:
Some injuries make it difficult or impossible to return to hobbies, activities, or routines that were once part of everyday life.
Wrongful Death Damages:
Families who lose a loved one in a fatal truck accident may be entitled to compensation for funeral expenses, loss of financial support, and loss of companionship.

In cases involving especially reckless behavior, additional damages may also be available. Because truck accident injuries are often severe, it is important to pursue compensation that fully accounts for both current and long-term needs.
Common Causes of Truck Accidents

The mistakes and careless actions of truck drivers cause a high proportion of truck accidents. These are not the only issues, however, that cause truck crashes. The actions of the following parties can also contribute to trucking accidents:
Trucking companies
Manufacturers of trucking equipment or parts
Manufacturers of trucks
Mechanics or maintenance technicians
Cargo loaders
Shippers
Transporters
Other drivers
Government agencies and contractors

Victims can make multiple liability claims for a truck accident. The victim’s attorney must perform a full investigation of any truck accident before a settlement offer is accepted. Otherwise, a claim may be settled for far less than its actual value.
What Makes a Truck Accident Different From a Car Accident?
A collision with a commercial truck is not the same as one with the average automobile. Truck accident cases have unique considerations, including different laws and types of evidence available. A
Denver truck accident lawyer
can walk you through all of how your case may differ, such as:

Federal trucking laws. Truck companies and their drivers have to obey federal safety rules, such as cargo securement requirements and hours-of-service regulations. Breaking these laws can contribute to truck accidents and make the truck company liable.
The size of the adversary. Trucking companies are powerful adversaries in accident lawsuits, making it even more important to have an attorney represent you.

Rapid response teams. Many truck companies deploy rapid response teams to immediately visit the scene of an accident and collect evidence. These teams typically consist of defense attorneys and investigators.

Unique types of evidence. The average truck accident involves evidence such as the truck’s black box, electronic logging devices, employment records, driving histories, truck inspection reports, and company compliance records.

No matter what unique elements your truck accident case entails, an attorney in Denver can help you fight for the best possible outcome. A lawyer will frame your argument based on the specific details of your accident.
Denver’s Highest-Risk Intersections
According to
transportation safety research published by TRIP, a national nonprofit that evaluates highway conditions and crash outcomes

, Colorado averages 697 traffic fatalities per year and records a fatality rate of 1.25 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles traveled. Against that backdrop, Denver’s highways consistently rank among the most dangerous in the state due to sustained congestion, rapid lane changes, and heavy freight traffic through urban interchanges. The most crash-prone areas center on I-25 and I-70, particularly where interstate traffic intersects with major city streets, creating conditions where large commercial trucks face limited stopping distance and reduced reaction time, leading to high-severity crashes.
For people searching for a
Denver truck accident lawyer

, these patterns matter because crashes along known high-risk corridors often involve complex investigations, disputed fault, and aggressive insurer defenses when commercial vehicles operate under tight delivery schedules. That local insight often separates a general personal injury practice from a firm that understands how these highways shape liability, evidence, and insurer behavior.
Interstate 25 (I-25) “The Valley Highway”

I-25 stands out as the most dangerous roadway in the Denver metro area, particularly through the central corridor, where commuter and truck traffic overlap. Between Speer Boulevard and Broadway, extreme congestion fuels rear-end crashes involving semis and delivery vehicles. Interchanges at West 6th Avenue report nearly 100 crashes annually as aggressive merging compresses traffic into short decision windows, while ramps at 20th Street near downtown and Coors Field see elevated collision rates tied to event traffic and restricted sight lines.

Southbound and northbound segments near East Hampden Avenue carry complex traffic volumes, increasing the likelihood of side-impact and underride crashes. The interchange at Yale Avenue continues to stand out as one of Denver’s most dangerous fatal crash locations, reinforcing why I-25 remains identified as the deadliest road in the city for severe and fatal truck collisions.
Interstate 70 (I-70)

I-70 presents a more violent risk profile driven by speed and freight density. Northeast Denver, between Quebec Street and E-470, has ranked as the deadliest ten-mile stretch in Colorado, recording 23 fatal crashes over a recent five-year period. Reports from 2024 and 2025 identify I-70 Eastbound at North Peoria Street as one of the most dangerous intersections in Denver, with more than 100 crashes recorded in a single year.

Additional high-risk segments extend from Wheat Ridge through central Denver, where long-haul trucks transition abruptly between highway speeds and urban traffic, increasing collision severity as braking distances shrink.
Other Dangerous Denver Corridors
As documented in
regional transportation planning materials published by Adams County

, several Denver-area corridors remain part of the region’s high-injury network due to freight volume, roadway design, and inconsistent pedestrian infrastructure. Federal Boulevard stands out for its combination of high truck traffic, sidewalk gaps, infrequent pedestrian crossings, and jurisdictional overlap, all of which raise the risk of severe collisions involving commercial vehicles.
Additional corridors contribute to Denver’s truck accident risk in ways insurers often overlook until a serious crash occurs:
A primary freight route feeding directly into I-70 and I-25, where merging trucks and commuter traffic frequently collide.
Particularly between East Smith Road and South Yosemite Street, where industrial traffic mixes with daily commuters.
A high-volume commuter corridor between Denver and Boulder that sees frequent rear-end crashes involving commercial vehicles.
Higher speeds increase the likelihood of catastrophic injuries when truck collisions happen.

Commercial Truck Rules and Regulations
The
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration

(FMCSA) governs commercial truck driving and drivers through a set of federal rules and regulations intended to prevent truck accidents, injuries, and deaths. Transportation companies and commercial truck drivers are required to follow these mandates.
FMCSA rules and regulations include the following:
Hours of service regulations require drivers to take regular breaks while on duty
Driver drug and alcohol testing
Maintenance, inspection, and repair requirements for commercial vehicles
Minimum insurance requirements
Minimum driver requirements
Forbids the use of handheld mobile phones
When truck drivers and their companies violate FMCSA policies, they open themselves to legal liability for truck accidents.
Who Might Be Liable for a Truck Accident?

Colorado is a fault-based insurance state. This means the driver at fault for the crash is typically financially responsible. However, with a truck accident, the rule of vicarious liability makes the trucking company legally responsible for the actions and mistakes of its drivers in most cases.

If the truck driver was working as an employee of the trucking company at the time that he or she negligently caused your crash, the trucking company will most likely bear vicarious liability for the accident. If someone else caused the accident, such as a cargo company or a third-party driver, that party might be liable instead. A lawyer can investigate your crash to determine liability.
How Long Do I Have to File a Lawsuit?

In Colorado, a law called a statute of limitations places a time limit on your right to bring a truck accident lawsuit. With only a few exceptions, you have two years to file a lawsuit after any type of accident that gives you a personal injury in Colorado. If you are only filing a claim for property damage and not a personal injury, however, you have three years from the date of your accident.

What to Do Immediately After a Truck Accident?
Unfortunately, trucking accidents happen frequently, particularly on major highways like I-70 and I-25. Driver error, poor maintenance, and fatigue all play a big part.

faqs.question: What Should Someone Do After a Colorado Truck Collision?

children.text: To collect evidence for the claim, you must call the police, get medical treatment, document the scene with photos and videos, avoid making statements to insurance companies, and get in touch with a truck accident attorney right away.

faqs.question: When Does a Truck Accident Need to Be Reported?

children.text: Right away. According to Colorado law, accidents involving serious injuries, deaths, or significant property damage must be reported to law enforcement.

faqs.question: What Evidence Is Used in a Truck Accident Case?

children.text: Police reports, driver logs, black box data, maintenance records, witness accounts, images, videos, and professional accident reconstructions are all examples of evidence from truck accidents.

faqs.question: How Is Negligence Determined in a Truck Accident Case?

children.text: To determine negligence in a case, you look at the driver’s behavior, business procedures (such as maintenance and training), logbooks, black box data, accident reconstructions, and expert analysis. This can be a primary reason a lawsuit is filed, and your case is taken to court, where a judge or a jury will decide.

faqs.question: Can I Sue Someone Personally After a Truck Accident?

children.text: Yes. Although you have the option to sue the negligent driver directly, the majority of damages are covered by the trucking company’s or the driver’s insurance. If insurance isn’t enough, personal assets might be used.

faqs.question: How Do Truck Accident Lawsuits Work?

children.text: Truck accident lawsuits typically start with an investigation of the truck accident, then it goes to identifying who is at fault (the driver, the trucking company, the manufacturer, etc.), negotiating with insurance companies, and finally filing a lawsuit if a fair settlement can’t be reached.

faqs.question: How Long Does an 18-Wheeler Lawsuit Take?

children.text: Depending on how complex the case is, and whether or not it goes to trial, these types of lawsuits usually last 18 months to three years.

faqs.question: Should I Accept a Settlement Offer?

children.text: A settlement offer is an amount of money an insurance company is offering you to end a claim. By accepting a settlement offer, you are agreeing to release the defendant of any further liability for your truck accident. Once you accept a settlement offer, you cannot renegotiate for a different amount. It is extremely important, therefore, to make sure you are settling for a fair amount before saying yes.

As a general rule, do not accept a settlement offer for a truck accident case without first consulting with an attorney. An insurance company’s initial offer is often much lower than the true value of the case. This is especially true if you have serious or catastrophic injuries that will require ongoing medical care or physical rehabilitation. A lawyer can review the offer and help you negotiate for a reasonable amount.

faqs.question: How Much Are Most Truck Accident Settlements?

children.text: Given the severity of truck accidents, settlements for these cases typically begin at $100,000 and can go up to millions for cases involving severe or catastrophic injuries.

faqs.question: How Much is My Truck Worth After an Accident?

children.text: The value of your truck after an accident is determined by the difference between the market value and the repair costs.
